memory_verse.label: Bible Reference
memory_verse.text: "Afterwards Moses and Aaron went to Pharaoh and said, "This is what the Lord, the God of Israel, says: 'Let my people go, so that they may hold a festival to me in the wilderness.'" Pharaoh said, "Who is the Lord, that I should obey him and let Israel go? I do not know the Lord and I will not let Israel go."" - Exodus 5:1-2 (NIV)

devotion.label: Devotion
devotion.text:
Moses delivers the message exactly as God gave it. Pharaoh's reply is one of the boldest sentences in Scripture: who is the Lord, that I should obey him?

It is not really a question. It is a dismissal. In Egypt, Pharaoh was regarded as divine himself. He had no category for a God who could give him orders, especially a God worshipped by slaves.

The whole book of Exodus becomes the answer to his question. Plague by plague, God will make Himself known — to Egypt, to Israel, and to every generation since.

It is worth noticing how modern this sounds. People still say it in different words: why should I answer to anyone? Who decides what is right for me? The instinct to resist any authority above ourselves is not an Egyptian problem. It is a human one.

The day is coming when every knee will bow and every tongue confess that Jesus Christ is Lord (Phil 2:10-11). The only question is whether we bow now, gladly, or later, unwillingly.

reflection.label: Reflection
reflection.text:
1. Is there an area of my life where I still say, "Who is the Lord that I should obey Him here?"
2. Have I fully surrendered my will, or only the parts that are convenient?

prayer.label: Prayer
prayer.text: Lord, I confess the places where I still want to be my own authority. Teach me to bow gladly to You today. Amen.
